label: Annelida
NameOrigin:
Annelida: From Latin annellus (“little ring”) ida.
Annelid translates to "little ringed ones;" literally, "little ring-shaped." Annel + id = "little ring" + "shape/form". Annelid comes from the French annelés "ringed ones", derived from the Latin annulus "little ring" (itself derived from anus "ring").

label: Arthropoda
NameOrigin:
Arthropoda: From Ancient Greek arthron (“joint”) + pous (“foot”) + -a (“neuter plural suffix”).
The word arthropod comes from the Greek árthron 'joint', and poús (gen. podós) 'foot' or 'leg', which together mean "jointed leg", with the word "arthropodes" initially used in anatomical descriptions by Barthélemy Charles Joseph Dumortier published in 1832. The designation "Arthropoda" appears to have been first used in 1843 by the German zoologist Johann Ludwig Christian Gravenhorst (1777–1857). The origin of the name has been the subject of considerable confusion, with credit often given erroneously to Pierre André Latreille or Karl Theodor Ernst von Siebold instead, among various others.

label: Crustacea
NameOrigin: Crustaceans (from Latin word "crustacea" meaning: "those with shells" or "crusted ones") are mandibulate arthropods that are traditionally a part of the paraphyletic subphylum Crustacea ().

label: Chelicerata
NameOrigin: Chelicerata: From Ancient Greek chele (“jawbone”) + keras (“horn”).

label: Malacostraca
NameOrigin:
Malacostraca: New Latin, from Ancient Greek malakostraka, from malakos (“soft”) + ostrakon (“shell”).
The name Malacostraca is from Ancient Greek malakos (malakós) 'soft' and ostrakon (óstrakon) 'shell'. The word was used by Aristotle, who contrasted them with oysters, in comparison with which their shells are pliable.

label: Amphipoda
NameOrigin:
Amphipoda: New Latin, from Ancient Greek amphi (“all over, all around”) + pous (“foot”).
The name Amphipoda comes, via Neo-Latin amphipoda, from the Greek roots amphi 'on both/all sides' and pous 'foot'. This contrasts with the related Isopoda, which have a single kind of thoracic leg. Particularly among anglers, amphipods are known as freshwater shrimp, scuds, or sideswimmers. The common names relate to their swimming habits, described as "scudding" and often having the animal tilt to one side.

label: Isopoda
NameOrigin:
Isopoda: iso- + -poda, New Latin, from Ancient Greek isos (“equal”) and pous (“foot”).
The name Isopoda is derived from the Greek roots iso- (from ísos, meaning "equal") and -pod (from pod-, the stem of poús, genitive podós, meaning "foot"). This refers to the fact that they have seven pairs of similarly shaped legs.

label: Caprellidae
facts1: Family of amphipod crustaceans with elongated slender bodies, typically clinging to algae or hydroids and moving in an inchworm fashion.

label: Cephalopoda
NameOrigin: Cephalopoda: From cephalo- + -poda, from Ancient Greek kephale (“head”) + pous (“foot”).

label: Megachelicerax
NameOrigin: The genus name is intended to mean “large chelicera” (chelicera literally meaning “claw-horn”) in Greek.

label: Animalia
NameOrigin:
Animalia: From Latin animal (“an animal, a living creature”).
The word animal comes from the Latin noun animal of the same meaning, which is itself derived from Latin animalis 'having breath or soul'. The biological definition includes all members of the kingdom Animalia. In colloquial usage, the term animal is often used to refer only to nonhuman animals. The term metazoa is derived from Ancient Greek meta 'after' (in biology, the prefix meta- stands for 'later') and zōia 'animals', plural of zōion 'animal'.

label: Gastropoda
NameOrigin: Gastropoda: gastro- + -poda, New Latin, from Ancient Greek gaster (“stomach”) and pous (“foot”).

label: Acanthochitonidae
authority: Simroth, 1894 (1881)  Introduced as a replacement name for Acanthochitidae, because its type genus, Acanthochites, is a synonym of Acanthochiton [emendation of Acanthochitona]. Ashby [1925, Proceedings of the Royal Society of Victoria, new ser., 37(2): 178] discussed the nomenclature of Acanthochitidae vs. Acanthochitonidae and concluded that they are two different names with different authorship; however he missed the earliest introductions of both names. This is a situation, covered by Art. 40; Acanthochitonidae is in prevailing usage, and is conserved with the precedence of Acanthochitidae (1881)

label: Anura
NameOrigin: A frog is any member of a diverse and largely semiaquatic group of short-bodied, tailless amphibian vertebrates composing the order Anura (coming from the Ancient Greek anoura, literally 'without tail').

label: Rhinopias frondosa
NameOrigin:
First described as Scorpaena frondosa.
The genus name is a combination of rhino meaning "snout" and op meaning "eye", an allusion to he upturned snout and raised orbits of R. frondosa with the suffix ias which is used in some Greek names for fishes, for example Xiphias.
The specific name frondosa means "branched or full of leaves", an allusion to the fleshy tentacles which cover most of the body of this fish.

label: Rhinopias
NameOrigin: The genus name is a combination of rhino meaning "snout" and op meaning "eye", an allusion to he upturned snout and raised orbits of R. frondosa with the suffix ias which is used in some Greek names for fishes, for example Xiphias.

label: Rhinopias aphanes

label: Ogcocephalus darwini
NameOrigin:
Ogcocephalus: From Ancient Greek onkos (“bulk, heap, weight; bend, angle, curve, hook”) + -cephalus (“head”).
The red-lipped batfish is a member of the genus Ogcocephalus (from Greek roots ogkos, "hook", and cephalus, "head"), an allusion to the pointed rostrum on the snout of the type species. The specific name refers to Charles Darwin, to mark the centenary of the publication of On the Origin of Species and to recognise the importance that the observations made on the Galápagos Islands had in developing the theory of island endemism.
